newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean minister denies monetary policy too tight.
newsitem.headline: Chilean minister denies monetary policy too tight.

text.p: Economy Minister Alvaro Garcia denied Tuesday that Central Bank policy was keeping the reins too tight on growth and said the year's inflation target was on track to be met.

Garcia, speaking after official figures showed a tiny 0.2 rise in consumer prices last year and a slight rise in unemployment, said he did not think the autonomous Central Bank's monetary policy would crimp growth into the second half of the year.

"Conditions are there for the Chilean economy to grow more quickly in the second half of the year (than in the first)," Garcia told reporters, repeating that he expects the economy to grow more than six percent in the second half of the year.
"We hope the Central Bank will work in accordance with those objectives," he said.

He noted that consumer inflation for the 12 months through May reached 5.4 percent, compared with the 5.5-6.0 percent target for all of calendar 1997 projected by the Central Bank and 5.8 percent projected by the government.

"We have a scenario in which the reaching of the inflation goal is highly probable," said Garcia. Higher wage levels, which in May rose 9.4 percent over the same month in 1996, were also encouraging, he said.
"We have an increase in remunerations which is coherent with increases in productivity, and for that reason it is not putting pressure on prices," he said.
In a welter of economic figures, the National Statistics Institute also reported that Chilean industrial output rose a modest 3.3 percent in April over the same month last year.
The Santiago stock exchange's blue-chip index was off 0.31 percent in afternoon trading and brokers said the decline, following a week-long rally, was due mainly to profit-taking.
